newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Shell chief confident of South China Sea peace.
newsitem.headline: Shell chief confident of South China Sea peace.

text.p: The chief of the Royal Dutch/Shell oil group has expressed confidence that oil and gas resources in the South China Sea can be developed peacefully despite competing territorial claims.

Cor Herkstroter, chairman of the oil major's committee of managing directors, made the comment during a visit to Australia where he affirmed the group's belief that the "breathtaking" opportunities in Asia outweighed potential regional problems.
"There could be (problems)," Herkstroter told reporters in a select media briefing before leaving the country on Saturday.
"But in the end everybody is interested in finding a solution I think, because if you have too many disputes then nothing (no development) will happen.
"So I am inclined to think something will be sorted out."

Herkstroter's confidence in the peaceful development of resources in the South China Sea comes as Southeast Asian nations and the United States are reported to have expressed disquiet over the scale of China's territorial claims there.

In July China called for joint development of disputed territories in the South China Sea after a political confrontation with the Philippines last year over a part of the hotly contested Spratly islands.
Thought to be rich in both oil and minerals, the islands are claimed in their entirety by China and Taiwan and in part by Malaysia, Vietnam, the Philippines and Brunei.

Vietnam, China and Taiwan also contest sovereignty of the nearby Paracel islands. In the gas-rich Natuna islands, off Indonesian Borneo, Jakarta staged war games this month after Beijing included the Natunas in a map of Chinese territory.
But Herkstroter said: "I believe that, in this region of the world, opportunities outweigh problems by a large margin."
He said the central economic theme in the region was growth, which would boost demand for oil, coal and gas.
"A good example is the gas industry," he told a private dinner held here earlier during his visit.

"The emergence of significant demand, primarily from a number of urban centres, from Jakarta in the south to Tokyo in the east and Bombay in the west, is likely to create the need for the most extensive gas pipeline network yet seen in the world."
He envisaged a gas pipeline network linking fields in Turkmenistan, Iran, Siberia, Sakhalin and the South China Sea with consumption centres for the gas scattered as widely.
"The scale of such a network is breathtaking," he said.
"Many of its component parts are already being built and any energy company that sees itself as a global player...must take part."
A meeting last month of Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum (APEC) energy officals highlighted the forecast surge in regional energy demand.

They were told that US$1.6 trillion of investment capital was needed to meet this demand over the next 10 years, and that the region was shifting increasingly to natural gas to fuel its energy sector.
Royal Dutch/Shell sells 1.5 million barrels of oil each day from its Asian operations and has stakes in 12 refineries in the region.
